This means that environmental factors and lifestyle choices can influence the expression of genes and potentially pass on these changes to future generations. Epigenetic changes can also occur spontaneously and may be reversible, which has implications for disease prevention and treatment. known as epigenetic inheritance. Unlike genetic inheritance, epigenetic inheritance involves changes in the expression of genes without any alteration in the DNA sequence itself. Epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation, histone modifications and non-coding RNA can be transmitted from one generation to another, affecting how the genes are expressed in the offspring, even if the DNA sequence remains the same. This can result in heritable traits and predisposition to certain diseases. However, the extent and duration of epigenetic inheritance is still not well understood, and more research is needed to investigate the factors that influence it.<|im_end|>

Commissioning the Northern Sky Array took the better part of two years. The site sits on a high plateau, far from the nearest town, and the road in is unpaved for the final forty kilometres. Engineers arrived in early March, when the ground was still frozen and the wind came down off the ridge in long, steady gusts.

Work began with the concrete pads. Each of the sixteen antenna stations needed a foundation level to within a millimetre, and the survey crew spent three weeks checking the forms before anyone poured. The first pad cracked during curing, which cost the project a fortnight and a long argument with the supplier. After that, the crew added a slow-setting additive and covered each pad with insulated blankets overnight.

The antennas themselves arrived by lorry in June. Assembly was straightforward but slow: each dish has forty-eight panels, and every panel is bolted by hand. Two students from the local technical college were hired for the summer and turned out to be the fastest workers on the site. By the end of July all sixteen dishes were standing, though only four had been aligned.

Power and data came next. A diesel generator ran the site for the first season, noisy and expensive, until the utility company finished the buried cable in October. The fibre runs from the control hut to each station through conduit laid in the same trench as the power, which saved a great deal of digging. Lightning arrestors were fitted at every entry point after a strike in August destroyed two switches.

The control hut is a small prefabricated building with two rooms: an equipment room and a cramped office with a kettle, a whiteboard and a window that does not open. The receivers live in the equipment room, rack-mounted and cooled by a pair of redundant fans. Temperature stability matters more than absolute temperature, so the fans run continuously and the door is kept shut.

Commissioning proper began in November, once the nights were long enough to give the team useful sky time. The first task was to confirm that each station reported a consistent clock. Timing errors of a few nanoseconds are enough to smear a correlation, and the early data were badly smeared. The fault turned out to be a firmware setting that reset the counters whenever the link dropped.

The software side was harder than anyone had expected. The correlator had been written for a smaller array and assumed that every station produced data at the same rate. On the new array the sample rates differ slightly, and the buffers slowly drift out of step. A rewrite of the scheduling layer fixed most of it, at the cost of a month's delay and a great deal of coffee.

By mid-December the array was producing usable fringes on the brightest calibrator sources. The team spent the last week of the year repeating the same observation over and over, changing one parameter at a time. On the final night, with snow on the ground and the generator droning in the background, the synchronisation of the timing beacons held for eleven hours without a single reset, and the engineers drove home satisfied.
